newsitem.title: USA: US farmers seen planting more soybeans this spring.
newsitem.headline: US farmers seen planting more soybeans this spring.

text.p: U.S. farmers look poised to increase plantings of soybeans this year, following a recent run-up in prices to 8-1/2 year highs, and to cut acreage devoted to spring wheat, analysts said.
"On paper, you could take two million acres out of spring wheat and put it in soybeans," said Dave Armstrong, grains analyst with ABN-AMRO Chicago Corp.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture is due to issue its first acreage estimate for spring planted crops on Monday at 0730 CST/1330 GMT. It will also issue estimates for grain and oilseed stocks as of March 1.
A Reuters survey of analysts produced an average forecast for U.S. soybean planted area this year of 65.85 million acres, up from 64.21 million in 1996.
Spring wheat area, excluding durum, was seen falling to an average 18.55 million acres from 20.04 million in 1996.
Soybean prices on the Chicago Board of Trade recently rose to an 8-1/2 year high of $8.67 a bushel on the May contract.

Spring wheat prices on the Minneapolis Grain Exchange, in contrast, have been on an overall downward trend since peaking in May 1996 at $7.32 a bushel. Nearby futures have recently stabilised around $4.00 a bushel.
Some analysts, however, suggested farmers may be slow to respond to the price incentive.
"Everyone is making the assumption that the farmer will quickly adapt to the new price structure, but history doesn't support that," Jerry Gidel, analyst with Dean Witter brokerage in Chicago said.
Because of this, Gidel said USDA would keep its soybean acreage forecast below 66 million acres in the report. He forecast 65.55 million.
The Reuters survey projected corn plantings at an average 80.92 million acres, up from 79.49 million in 1996.
Prudential Securities oilseed analyst Anne Frick noted most of the land switched to soybeans from corn last year because of wet weather would be replanted to corn this year.
"The odds are against it being put back into beans because of rotational considerations," she said.
Analysts will also be closely monitoring the quarterly stocks report, with soybeans the main focus given the current tightness in U.S. supplies.
"The grain stocks report shouldn't have the firepower it had last year, but this bean report could give us a bit of a tweak," said Dean Witter's Gidel.
The Reuters survey produced an average soybean stocks estimate, as of March 1, of 1.093 billion bushels, down from USDA's estimate for a year earlier of 1.190 billion.

"If for some reason we go down to 1.075 (billion bushels), that means there's a chance we overestimated the crop," Gidel said. "We don't have bushels to spare. There's no extra beans out here. We can't afford to put 20 million (bushels) of beans into the system between now and September 1."
Corn stocks were seen rising to an average 4.565 billion bushels from 3.800 million a year earlier, while wheat stocks were seen little changed at 827 million versus 823 million.
"We still have plenty of corn. We're not running out of corn any time soon," Gidel said.
"Wheat seems unexciting," he added.
((Chicago newsdesk 312-408 8720))
